To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

employers are concerned about the costs of employing people with disabilities and that these concerns are unfounded; employers are concerned about their ability to accommodate people with disabilities in the workplace and that these concerns also are unfounded; and employers are concerned about productivity and performance and that these concerns, too, are unfounded

employers' concerns about the employment related abilities of people who have disabilities are often based on inaccurate and incomplete information, and that the employment related abilities that are most commonly cited by employers as being problematic are actually not problematic, and that the evidence based solutions to employers' concerns can be implemented at relatively low cost.

People with disabilities are less likely than people without disabilities to be employed, but those who are employed have similar or better performance than people without disabilities; People with disabilities are not more likely to have negative absenteeism or turnover rates than people without disabilities, but they are less likely to be promoted to management positions
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the experiences of people with disabilities in the workplace and the ways in which their experiences are shaped by the attitudes of others.
the participation of people with disabilities in the workplace.
the question of how employers can be better informed about the abilities of people with and without disabilities so that all employees can be treated equitably and fairly.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
people with disabilities can work and can work well, and that the employment cycle is not an insurmountable barrier.

the research evidence supports a strong case for the inclusion of people with disabilities in the workplace and that the evidence refutes the majority of the employer concerns about the employment related abilities of people who have disabilities.
the evidence supports the view that the participation of people with disabilities in employment, in all its forms, is not only desirable and beneficial, but also feasible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence supports a more positive view of people with disabilities in the workplace than is currently held by many employers.
people with disabilities have the same abilities as their peers without disabilities.
the research evidence supports the view that people with disabilities are capable of contributing to the workplace in a variety of ways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
employers need to be more proactive in creating and implementing effective strategies that address the needs of people with disabilities.

the employment of people with disabilities is a complex issue that requires an understanding of the interrelated concerns of employers and employees and a commitment to creating workplaces that are inclusive of all individuals.
employers need to move beyond the myths and misconceptions that they have about people with disabili ties and embrace the reality that people with disabilities are a valuable and untapped resource.
